title: Why It Sucks to Be Born as a Mayfly (Part 1) - TikTok pilot sample 10/27
_note: Lab 07 series pilot: Meatball IS the mayfly ('you'), narration from 0 s, escalation rough -> worse -> absurd, opinion poll ~10-12 s, one follow ask in the last 3-5 s tied to the series. Rendered on the 10/27 renderer defaults, v3 stills (v4 cut-outs of small insects stay tiny under the 1.5x cap). Photos: iNaturalist, CC0/CC BY only, credited. No swarm/bridge photo with a usable licence was reachable (Commons rate-limited), so those lines play over mayfly photos with labels.

series.text: WHY IT SUCKS TO BE BORN AS...

sources: Adults don't feed; mouthparts vestigial/non-functional; gut filled with air: Texas A&M AgriLife Field Guide (texasinsects.tamu.edu/ephemeroptera/), NC State Insect ID (genent.cals.ncsu.edu/insect-identification/order-ephemeroptera)

Nymphs live underwater about 1-2 years; the only insects that molt again after getting working wings (subimago -> imago): PNAS commentary (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8463790), Missouri Dept. of Conservation field guide (mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/mayfly-larvae)
Adults live from a couple of hours to a day or two, none longer than ~3 days: Illinois DNR (dnr.illinois.gov ... mayfly.pdf)
Female Dolania americana: under 5 minutes as an adult: Univ. of Florida Book of Insect Records ch. 37 (entnemdept.ufl.edu/walker/ufbir/chapters/chapter_37.shtml)
Mayfly swarms on NWS weather radar (La Crosse 2014; Cleveland/Detroit): Christian Science Monitor 2014-07-25; Cleveland Magazine
June 2015: swarm closed the Route 462 Columbia-Wrightsville bridge, PA; bulldozers cleared the piles: Science News; WITF 2015-06-15; AP
Ephemeroptera from Greek ephemeros 'lasting a day' + pteron 'wing'; fly anglers tie mayfly imitations: Wikipedia 'Mayfly' (etymology), common fly-fishing practice
Male mayflies have large eyes for spotting females in swarms; first winged stage (subimago/dun) has dull, cloudy wings: Wikipedia 'Mayfly'; Missouri Dept. of Conservation
Mayflies are pollution-sensitive; big swarms indicate clean water (NWS Cleveland via Cleveland Magazine; CSM 2014)

beats.say: You're a mayfly. You spent a year or two underwater, eating algae in the dark.
Finally, you grow wings. Time to live!
Bad news. You get a day. Maybe two.
Years of mud, for a day of flying. Worth it? Comment.
And you can't eat. Your mouth doesn't even work.
Your stomach? Full of air.
So you get one job. Find a mate. Fast.
If you're a male, you even get giant eyes, just to spot females in the swarm.
But first, you have to molt. Again. After you can already fly.
No other insect does that. Your first wings come out dull. So you crawl out of your own skin, wings and all.
Now everything wants to eat you. Fish. Birds. Bats.
People even tie fake versions of you, to catch fish.
And you're not alone. Millions of you hatch on the same night.
So many, you show up on weather radar. Like a storm.
In 2015, a swarm of you closed a bridge in Pennsylvania.
They brought in bulldozers to clear the piles.
And if you're a female Dolania mayfly?
You get less than five minutes.
Five minutes. To mate, lay your eggs, and die.
Scientists even named you after it. Ephemeroptera. Wings for a day.
The one upside? Big swarms of you mean the river is clean.
That was Why It Sucks to Be Born as a Mayfly. Part one.
Follow for the next animal.
